subChunks.title: Stack vs Heap Memory
subChunks.hookHtml: Why does calling a method not corrupt your variables? Why does creating a thousand objects not run out of memory immediately? The answer lies in how Java divides and manages its two main memory regions: the stack and the heap.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Stack Memory

The stack is a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) structure. It holds:

  • Local primitive variables (int x = 5)
  • Local reference variables (the pointer to an object, not the object itself)
  • Method call frames — when a method is called, a new frame is pushed; when it returns, the frame is popped

Stack access is fast and automatic — the frame disappears when the method ends. Stack memory is limited (typically 512KB–1MB). A very deep recursion causes a StackOverflowError.

Heap Memory

The heap is a larger, unordered region that holds:

  • All objects created with new
  • Arrays
  • String objects (though string literals go in the string pool, a special region of the heap)

Objects on the heap persist until the Garbage Collector reclaims them.

Primitives vs References

int x = 42;               // primitive — value lives on the stack
String s = "hello";       // reference on stack; object on heap
int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};   // reference on stack; array on heap

int a = 10;
int b = a;  // b gets a COPY of 10 — changing b does not affect a
b = 99;
System.out.println(a); // still 10

int[] arr1 = {1, 2, 3};
int[] arr2 = arr1; // arr2 points to the SAME array!
arr2[0] = 99;
System.out.println(arr1[0]); // 99 — arr1 also changed!

This distinction — value semantics for primitives, reference semantics for objects — is one of the most important concepts in Java.

storyBeats.text: Eldrin takes you to the Academy's magical library — two wings, divided by a glass wall. The left wing is tiny but blazingly fast; the right wing is vast but takes a moment to navigate.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The left wing is the stack — small, ordered, lightning-fast. Every time you call a method, a new shelf appears at the top. Local variables are placed on that shelf. When the method returns, the entire shelf vanishes — no cleanup needed.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The right wing is the heap — vast, unordered, holding every object you create with new. The stack holds only a reference — a magical pointer — to the heap object. The object itself lives on the heap until the garbage collector claims it.

storyBeats.speaker: Stack vs heap
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This creates the most important distinction in Java: value semantics versus reference semantics. Copying a primitive gives you an independent duplicate. Copying a reference gives you a second pointer to the same object.

storyBeats.speaker: The reference trap

options: Stack
Heap
String pool

questions.explanationHtml: Objects created with new are allocated on the heap. The reference to the object (the variable) lives on the stack, but the actual object data is on the heap.
Primitives use value semantics — y gets a copy of x's value. Changing y does not affect x.

questions.questionHtml: Two variables reference the same array. If you modify the array through one variable, what happens when you read via the other?
options: The other variable still has the old values
The other variable sees the updated values
A ConcurrentModificationException is thrown
The array is copied automatically
questions.correctAnswer: The other variable sees the updated values
questions.explanationHtml: Arrays are objects stored on the heap. Both variables hold references (pointers) to the same memory. Modifying the array through one reference is immediately visible through the other.

questions.questionHtml: A developer sees this and is confused that the value is unchanged. What is the bug?
questions.correctAnswer: Java passes primitives by value. addFive gets a copy of n; changing that copy does not affect the caller's variable. To return a modified value, the method should return int and the caller should reassign: value = addFive(value);
questions.explanationHtml: Java is always pass-by-value. For primitives, the method receives a copy of the value. Modifications inside the method do not affect the original variable. For objects, the method receives a copy of the reference — you can mutate the object through it, but reassigning the reference variable inside the method does not affect the caller's reference.

subChunks.title: Garbage Collection Concepts
subChunks.hookHtml: In C, programmers manually free memory. Forgetting causes memory leaks. In Java, an automated system called the Garbage Collector handles cleanup — but understanding it prevents subtle performance bugs.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is Garbage Collection?

The Garbage Collector (GC) automatically reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from any live reference. You never call free() in Java — the JVM handles it.

When is an object eligible for GC?

Wizard w = new Wizard("Lyria", 100); // object on heap, w references it
w = null;                            // w no longer references the object
// the Wizard object is now eligible for GC

// OR: reference goes out of scope
void createWizard() {
    Wizard temp = new Wizard("Temp", 10);
    // temp goes out of scope when method ends — object eligible for GC
}

GC Roots

An object is reachable if there is a chain of references from a GC root to it. GC roots include: local variables on the stack, static fields, and JNI references. Everything else is collectible.

Generational GC

Modern JVMs divide the heap into generations:

  • Young generation — newly created objects (Eden space + Survivor spaces). Most objects die young — GC here is fast.
  • Old generation (Tenured) — objects that survived several young-GC cycles. Collected less frequently.

This matches the observation that most objects are short-lived (e.g., a loop variable, a temporary result).

Avoiding memory leaks in Java

Java can still leak memory if you hold unintended references:

// A growing static list holds references forever
static List<byte[]> held = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    held.add(new byte[1_000_000]); // 1 MB each — never collected!
}

Always remove references you no longer need: clear collections, close resources with try-with-resources.

Note on finalize(): finalize() is deprecated for removal in Java 21 and must not be used in new code. For deterministic cleanup, implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources. For GC-triggered cleanup when try-with-resources is not applicable (e.g. wrapping a native resource), register a java.lang.ref.Cleaner action:

// finalize() is deprecated for removal — use Cleaner instead
private static final java.lang.ref.Cleaner CLEANER = java.lang.ref.Cleaner.create();
private final java.lang.ref.Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

MyResource() {
    cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, () -> System.out.println("Resource cleaned up"));
}

storyBeats.text: Deep below the Academy, enchanted automata silently patrol the vaults, dissolving conjurations that no wizard is still holding.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Unlike the old days when wizards had to dissolve their own constructs — and some forgot, causing catastrophic overloads — Java employs Garbage Collectors. Any object that no wizard is still pointing to is dissolved automatically.

storyBeats.speaker: Making an object eligible
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The GC finds collectible objects by walking from roots — the live variables on the stack and static fields. Anything reachable is safe. Everything else is claimed.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Java's GC is generational. Most objects are short-lived — a loop counter, a builder, a temporary result. These live in the young generation and are cleared rapidly. Objects that survive long enough are promoted to the old generation, collected less frequently but more thoroughly.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But never be complacent. Even in Java, you can leak memory by holding references you no longer need — a static collection that grows forever, an event listener never deregistered. The GC cannot collect what is still referenced.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
This exercise is observational — we'll demonstrate reachability with a simulation using a simple tracking class.

Write a class TrackedObject with a String label field, a constructor, and a close() method that prints "[label] closed". Use try-with-resources to ensure the object is closed automatically by implementing AutoCloseable.

Note: finalize() is deprecated for removal in Java 21. The modern approach for cleanup actions is to implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources, or to register a java.lang.ref.Cleaner action for cases where try-with-resources is not applicable.

In main: use a try-with-resources block to create a TrackedObject named "Alpha" — the close method will be called automatically. Then create TrackedObject b = new TrackedObject("Beta") and print b.label. Finally, print "Done".

questions.questionHtml: When does an object become eligible for garbage collection?
options: When the programmer calls System.gc()
When no live references point to it
When the JVM runs out of heap space
After 30 seconds of inactivity
questions.correctAnswer: When no live references point to it
questions.explanationHtml: An object is eligible for GC when it is no longer reachable — no chain of references from any GC root leads to it. System.gc() is only a hint, not a guarantee.

questions.questionHtml: Java's garbage collector guarantees that memory will be freed at a predictable point in time.
questions.explanationHtml: The GC runs at its own discretion, not on a predictable schedule. System.gc() is a hint that may be ignored. You cannot rely on finalize() being called at a specific time.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following can cause a memory leak in Java despite the GC?
options: Using local variables inside a method
Adding objects to a static List and never removing them
Creating objects inside a loop that terminates
Passing objects to methods as arguments
questions.correctAnswer: Adding objects to a static List and never removing them
questions.explanationHtml: A static field is a GC root. Objects held in a static collection remain reachable forever — the GC cannot collect them even if your code never uses them again. This is the most common source of memory leaks in Java applications.

questions.questionHtml: Why does Java's GC use generational collection (young + old generation) rather than a single scan of the whole heap?
options: To support multiple threads
Because most objects die young — frequent short scans of the young generation are cheaper than scanning everything
To support both stack and heap
Java's GC is not generational
questions.correctAnswer: Because most objects die young — frequent short scans of the young generation are cheaper than scanning everything
questions.explanationHtml: Empirical data shows most objects are short-lived (temporary variables, builders, DTOs). Collecting only the young generation frequently is cheap and reclaims the vast majority of garbage. Long-lived objects are promoted to the old generation and collected less frequently, avoiding the cost of scanning stable objects over and over.

subChunks.title: Reflection API
subChunks.hookHtml: Every Java class carries a blueprint of itself — fields, methods, constructors — locked inside a Class object. Reflection is the key that opens it, letting frameworks inspect and manipulate code they've never seen at compile time.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Obtaining a Class Object

There are three ways to get a Class<T> object — the entry point for all reflection.

// 1. Class literal — compile-time, type-safe, no exception
Class<String> c1 = String.class;

// 2. Instance method — from a live object
String s = "hello";
Class<?> c2 = s.getClass();

// 3. Class.forName() — runtime lookup by fully qualified name
//    Throws ClassNotFoundException if not found
Class<?> c3 = Class.forName("java.lang.String");

System.out.println(c1.getSimpleName()); // "String"
System.out.println(c1 == c2);          // true — same Class object

Inspecting Fields and Methods

getDeclaredFields() returns all fields declared in the class (including private ones). getFields() returns only public fields, including inherited ones. The same distinction applies to getDeclaredMethods() vs getMethods().

class Spell {
    private String name;
    private int power;
    Spell(String name, int power) { this.name = name; this.power = power; }
}

Class<?> clazz = Spell.class;

// Print all declared field names
for (Field field : clazz.getDeclaredFields()) {
    System.out.println("Field: " + field.getName() + " (" + field.getType().getSimpleName() + ")");
}

// Print all declared method names
for (Method method : clazz.getDeclaredMethods()) {
    System.out.println("Method: " + method.getName());
}

Accessing Private Fields with setAccessible

Private fields normally block reflective access. field.setAccessible(true) bypasses the access check — powerful but use with care. This is how many serialisation frameworks and ORMs read private fields.

Spell spell = new Spell("Fireball", 90);
Field nameField = Spell.class.getDeclaredField("name");
nameField.setAccessible(true); // bypass private access check
String value = (String) nameField.get(spell); // read the private field
System.out.println(value); // "Fireball"

// Writing to a private field:
nameField.set(spell, "Blizzard");
System.out.println((String) nameField.get(spell)); // "Blizzard"

Invoking Methods and Creating Instances

Reflection can also call methods and construct objects dynamically — critical for dependency injection frameworks.

// Creating an instance via Constructor
Constructor<?> ctor = Spell.class.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class, int.class);
ctor.setAccessible(true);
Spell newSpell = (Spell) ctor.newInstance("Thunder", 75);

// Invoking a method dynamically
Method method = String.class.getMethod("toUpperCase");
String result = (String) method.invoke("fireball"); // "FIREBALL"
System.out.println(result);

Costs and Risks of Reflection

Reflection is powerful but carries real costs: Performance — reflective calls bypass JIT optimisations, roughly 10-100x slower than direct calls. Type safety — errors appear at runtime, not compile time. Encapsulation — bypasses access modifiers, violating information hiding. Security — restricted by SecurityManager in some environments. Use reflection sparingly and only where it provides irreplaceable value (frameworks, testing, serialisation).

// Prefer direct access when possible:
spell.getName(); // fast, type-safe, clear

// Use reflection only when the type is unknown at compile time:
void inspect(Object obj) {
    for (Field f : obj.getClass().getDeclaredFields()) {
        f.setAccessible(true);
        System.out.println(f.getName() + " = " + f.get(obj));
    }
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy's ancient Registry claimed it could tell you everything about any scroll, any artifact, any spell — without ever having opened them before. The secret was the Reflection Codex: a mirror that showed a class's own blueprint.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every Java class carries a Class object — a runtime descriptor of its own structure. With reflection, you can read that descriptor to discover fields, methods, and constructors you never knew existed at compile time.

storyBeats.speaker: Getting a Class Object
storyBeats.text:
Class<?> clazz = Spell.class; // or spell.getClass()
System.out.println(clazz.getSimpleName()); // "Spell"

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: getDeclaredFields reveals every field — even the private ones. But touching them requires setAccessible(true), a powerful incantation that bypasses the normal wards of encapsulation. Use it only when the need is genuine.

storyBeats.speaker: Reading a Private Field
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Spring, Hibernate, Jackson — these mighty frameworks use reflection at their core. They never know your class names at compile time. At runtime, they peer into your classes and wire everything together.

The Registry hummed with power. Given any artifact — a Spell, a Record, a config class — it could print every field name and value, construct new instances, and call methods by name. The mirror of code had revealed all secrets.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Every type in Java has exactly one Class object per classloader, representing its runtime type descriptor. It's the entry point for all reflection operations.
getDeclaredFields() returns all fields of THIS class (including private) but not inherited ones. getFields() returns all public fields including inherited ones from superclasses.
Bypasses Java's access control check for the specific Field/Method/Constructor. On Java 9+, module boundaries may still restrict this — modules must explicitly open packages for deep reflection.
Java 9 modules restrict reflective access to private members across module boundaries. Libraries like Hibernate must explicitly open their modules or be placed in unnamed modules.
java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle (Java 7+) provides faster, type-safe reflective access than the traditional Field/Method API. Used internally by the JVM for lambda implementation and invokedynamic.
java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates implementations of interfaces at runtime using reflection. Spring's AOP and many mocking frameworks use dynamic proxies to intercept method calls.

Jackson serialises/deserialises JSON using reflection to discover fields and their types at runtime. It reads @JsonProperty annotations to map JSON keys to field names without compile-time knowledge of your class.
The mechanism that loads class bytecode into the JVM. Each Class object is associated with the ClassLoader that loaded it. Custom ClassLoaders enable hot-reloading and plugin systems.

questions.questionHtml: Which method returns ALL fields of a class including private ones, but excludes inherited fields?
options: getFields()
getDeclaredFields()
getAllFields()
getPrivateFields()
questions.explanationHtml: getDeclaredFields() returns every field declared in this class (public, protected, package, private) but not fields from superclasses. getFields() returns only public fields, including inherited ones.
getSimpleName() returns "Potion". getDeclaredField("potency") gets the potency field; setAccessible(true) allows reading; f.get(p) returns 75.

questions.questionHtml: This reflection code throws an exception. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
questions.correctAnswer: Add f.setAccessible(true) before calling f.get(spell) to bypass the private access check
questions.explanationHtml: Accessing a private field via reflection without calling setAccessible(true) throws IllegalAccessException. Add f.setAccessible(true); after getting the field and before calling f.get(spell).

questions.questionHtml: When is using reflection justified over direct code?
options: Whenever you want to avoid writing boilerplate getter methods
When the class name or field name is not known at compile time, such as in a generic serialisation framework
When performance is critical — reflection is faster than direct method calls
When you want to access static fields only
questions.correctAnswer: When the class name or field name is not known at compile time, such as in a generic serialisation framework
questions.explanationHtml: Reflection's only legitimate advantage is handling unknown types at compile time. For known types, direct access is always preferable: it's faster, type-safe, and clear. Reflection is slower than direct calls, not faster — it bypasses JIT optimisations.

subChunks.title: Custom Annotations
subChunks.hookHtml: Annotations are metadata woven into the fabric of your code — invisible at runtime unless you read them with reflection. They power Spring's component scanning, JUnit's test discovery, and Jackson's JSON mapping.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Defining a Custom Annotation

Annotations are defined with @interface. Elements are declared like methods; provide default values with default. Elements without defaults must be provided at the use site.

@interface SpellMeta {
    String school() default "Unknown";
    int tier() default 1;
    boolean experimental() default false;
}

// Usage:
@SpellMeta(school = "Fire", tier = 3)
class Inferno {
    // class body
}

Retention Policies

@Retention controls when the annotation is available. This is critical — choose the wrong policy and you won't be able to read it at the time you need it.

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE)  // only in source; discarded by compiler
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.CLASS)   // kept in .class file; not at runtime (default)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) // available at runtime via reflection ← use this!

// Example:
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) // MUST be RUNTIME to read via reflection
@interface SpellMeta {
    String school() default "Unknown";
    int tier() default 1;
}

Target — Where the Annotation Can Be Applied

@Target restricts which code elements the annotation may appear on. Omitting @Target means it can go anywhere.

import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;

@Target({ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD})
@interface SpellMeta {
    // This annotation is only valid on types or methods
    // Applying it to a field causes a compile error
    String school() default "Unknown";
    int tier() default 1;
}

// ElementType options:
// TYPE, FIELD, METHOD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR,
// LOCAL_VARIABLE, ANNOTATION_TYPE, PACKAGE, MODULE

Reading Annotations at Runtime via Reflection

With @Retention(RUNTIME), you can read annotations at runtime using getAnnotation() or isAnnotationPresent().

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@interface SpellMeta {
    String school() default "Unknown";
    int tier() default 1;
}

@SpellMeta(school = "Fire", tier = 3)
class Inferno {}

// Reading it:
Class<?> clazz = Inferno.class;
if (clazz.isAnnotationPresent(SpellMeta.class)) {
    SpellMeta meta = clazz.getAnnotation(SpellMeta.class);
    System.out.println("School: " + meta.school()); // "School: Fire"
    System.out.println("Tier: "   + meta.tier());   // "Tier: 3"
}

Real-World Annotation Use Cases

Annotations are used everywhere in modern Java: @SpringBootApplication triggers component scanning; @Test marks JUnit test methods; @JsonProperty renames JSON fields; @Column maps fields to DB columns; @Validated triggers Bean Validation. Behind each one is reflection code reading the annotation and acting on it at runtime (or compile time for SOURCE-retained ones like @Override and Lombok annotations).

// @Override is SOURCE-retained — compiler checks, then discards
@Override
public String toString() { return "Spell"; }

// @NonNull in Lombok is also SOURCE — generates null checks at compile time
// @Entity in JPA is CLASS or RUNTIME — Hibernate reads it to map tables

storyBeats.text: The Academy needed a way to mark every spell with its school and power tier — metadata that frameworks could read automatically without requiring every mage to write inspection code by hand. The answer lay in the art of annotation.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: An annotation is a label stitched into the very fabric of a class. It carries no logic itself — but frameworks that find it can read its values and act accordingly.

storyBeats.speaker: Defining an Annotation
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Retention is everything. SOURCE annotations dissolve after compilation. CLASS annotations persist in the bytecode but remain invisible to running programs. Only RUNTIME annotations can be read by the reflection spells we mastered in the last lesson.

storyBeats.speaker: Reading an Annotation
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Spring, JUnit, Jackson — their magic is largely annotations read at runtime. You write @Component, Spring reads it. You write @Test, JUnit reads it. Now you know how they perform that feat.

The Registry now catalogued itself. Each spell class bore its @SpellMeta label, and the framework read every label at startup — building the entire school hierarchy automatically without a single line of explicit registration code.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A meta-annotation controlling annotation lifetime. SOURCE: compile-time only. CLASS: in bytecode but not runtime. RUNTIME: readable via reflection. Always use RUNTIME for framework processing.
A meta-annotation restricting which code elements an annotation may appear on: TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, etc. Omitting @Target means the annotation is unrestricted.
Annotations that annotate other annotations. @Retention, @Target, @Documented, @Inherited, and @Repeatable are the standard meta-annotations defined in java.lang.annotation.
Allows the same annotation to be applied multiple times to the same element. Requires a container annotation type that holds an array of the repeatable annotation.
A compile-time tool (javax.annotation.processing.Processor) that reads SOURCE or CLASS-retained annotations and generates code or validates constraints. Used by Lombok, MapStruct, and Dagger.
A standard annotation-based validation framework. @NotNull, @Size, @Min, @Email — each is a RUNTIME-retained annotation read by a validator (like Hibernate Validator) to enforce constraints.
A meta-annotation indicating the annotated annotation should appear in Javadoc. Annotations are excluded from Javadoc by default unless @Documented is present.
When present, a class-level annotation is automatically inherited by subclasses. Only works for class annotations — method and field annotations are never inherited.

questions.questionHtml: Which retention policy must you use for an annotation that should be readable at runtime via reflection?
options: RetentionPolicy.SOURCE
RetentionPolicy.CLASS
RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME
RetentionPolicy.REFLECT
questions.explanationHtml: RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME keeps the annotation in the bytecode AND makes it accessible via the reflection API. SOURCE annotations are discarded by the compiler; CLASS annotations are in bytecode but not accessible at runtime.
The @Tag annotation has RUNTIME retention, so getAnnotation() returns it. t.value() returns "arcane" as specified at the use site.

questions.questionHtml: This code always prints "missing" even though the annotation is applied. What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: Add @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) to @interface SpellMeta — without it, the annotation is not available at runtime
questions.explanationHtml: Without @Retention, the default policy is CLASS — the annotation exists in bytecode but is NOT accessible via reflection at runtime. getAnnotation() returns null. Add @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) to fix it.

questions.questionHtml: You are writing a validation annotation like @NotBlank that should be checked at compile time AND at runtime. Which approach is correct?
options: Use RetentionPolicy.SOURCE only — compile-time tools handle it all
Use RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME only — it's accessible at both compile and runtime
Use RetentionPolicy.CLASS — this is the broadest policy
Use RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME for runtime validation and also write an annotation processor for compile-time checks
questions.correctAnswer: Use RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME for runtime validation and also write an annotation processor for compile-time checks
questions.explanationHtml: RUNTIME retention is needed for runtime validators (e.g., Hibernate Validator calling validate()). For compile-time checks (IDE warnings, static analysis), you'd additionally write an annotation processor. SOURCE-only annotations like @Override are fully discarded after compilation and never available at runtime.
